common.hidden: Submit your prediction to unlock the plot. The plot is not the answer; it is there to test your reasoning.

prediction.title: Predict first, then look
prediction.description: Use the formula and the parameters to commit to an answer, and write down why. The plot appears only after you submit.
prediction.reasonPlaceholder: For example: because the real part of the pole is negative, the envelope decays as e^{σt}, so ...
prediction.reasonHint: Write at least {count} characters. A because-therefore sentence is more useful than a bare conclusion.
prediction.noPenalty: A wrong answer is not penalised, but you must resubmit your reasoning.
prediction.correctHint: The plot is unlocked. Check that your reasoning explains the key feature of the curve.
prediction.incorrectHint: The plot is unlocked. Before changing your answer, find the part that contradicts your prediction.

fourierTransform.title: Fourier transform: pulse and sinc
fourierTransform.subtitle: A narrower pulse gives a wider main lobe; the pulse area sets the DC value. Drag the width and watch time and frequency trade places.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.description: x(t) is a rectangle of width τ and height A, centred at the origin.
controls.widthHint: Changing the width moves the spectral zeros.
controls.amplitudeHint: The height only scales the result linearly.

readouts.dcHint: Equal to the pulse area Aτ
readouts.areaHint: Aτ sets the overall spectral height

plot.timeDescription: The shaded area is Aτ, which is also X(0).
plot.spectrumDescription: The dashed line marks the first zero. Side lobes decay as frequency grows.

insight.title: What to notice
insight.duality: Rectangle ↔ sinc is a fundamental pair: the boxier the time signal, the more spread-out the spectrum.
insight.scaling: Halve τ and the main lobe doubles in width; double A and the whole spectrum doubles in height.
insight.zeros: Zeros sit at f = k/τ (k = ±1, ±2, ...), not at arbitrary frequencies.
insight.uncertainty: A narrow time signal needs a wide band. This is the signals version of an uncertainty principle.

experiment.title: Try this
experiment.narrow: Move τ from 2 s to 0.5 s. Predict whether the main lobe widens or narrows.
experiment.predict: Compute 1/τ first, then check the first zero on the plot.
experiment.connect: Fix τ and change only A: the zeros stay put while the height scales.

laplace.title: Laplace transform: poles and the ROC
laplace.subtitle: Drag a conjugate pole pair across the imaginary axis: left half-plane decays, the axis oscillates, the right half-plane grows. The ROC decides causality and stability.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.description: The poles are at σ ± jω. This lab assumes a causal system, so the ROC lies to the right of the rightmost pole.
controls.sigmaHint: σ < 0 is stable, σ = 0 is marginal, σ > 0 is unstable.
controls.omegaHint: ω sets the oscillation rate; |σ| sets how fast the envelope decays or grows.

readouts.stabilityHint: Check whether every pole is in the left half-plane
readouts.decayTitle: Read the response from the poles
readouts.decayDescription: The real part controls the envelope and the imaginary part controls oscillation; together they determine h(t).
readouts.excludesAxis: Does not include the jω axis

plot.pzDescription: The shaded region is to the right of the rightmost pole; a causal ROC extends to the right.
plot.impulseDescription: The envelope is e^{σt}; ω controls the oscillation.
plot.clipped: Peak is about {peak}; the vertical axis is clipped.

insight.title: What to notice
insight.left: A left half-plane pole gives an e^{σt} decaying envelope: stable.
insight.axis: A simple pole on the imaginary axis gives constant oscillation: marginal.
insight.right: A right half-plane pole gives a growing envelope: unstable.
insight.roc: The ROC contains the jω axis if and only if the system is stable. For a causal system the ROC is to the right of the rightmost pole.

experiment.title: Try this
experiment.cross: Move σ from −2 to 1 slowly. Predict how the envelope of h(t) changes.
experiment.omega: Fix σ and change only ω: the oscillation gets denser while the envelope stays the same.
experiment.roc: At σ = 0, does the ROC still contain the jω axis? Is the system stable?

secondOrder.title: Second-order systems: damping decides
secondOrder.subtitle: ζ controls overshoot and ωn controls speed. Move from underdamped to overdamped and watch peak time and settling time.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.description: ζ is the damping ratio and ωn is the undamped natural frequency. The step response settles at 1.
controls.zetaHint: ζ < 1 is underdamped, ζ = 1 is critical, ζ > 1 is overdamped.
controls.naturalFrequencyHint: A larger ωn makes the whole response faster.

plot.title: Step response
plot.description: The dashed line is the final value 1; the marker is the first peak.

insight.title: What to notice
insight.under: A smaller ζ means more overshoot and ringing, but a faster rise.
insight.critical: At ζ = 1 there is no overshoot: the fastest response without overshoot.
insight.over: For ζ > 1 there is no overshoot, but the two real poles separate and the response slows down.
insight.natural: Fix ζ and increase ωn: the whole response is compressed in time.

experiment.title: Try this
experiment.fixed: Fix ωn = 2 and move ζ from 0.1 to 1.0, recording the overshoot.
experiment.cross: Set ζ exactly to 1 and confirm that the overshoot is zero.
experiment.compare: Compare the settling time at ζ = 0.5 and ζ = 2, and explain why overdamped is not always faster.

modulation.title: Modulation: moving the spectrum to a carrier
modulation.subtitle: Use a baseband cosine to control the carrier amplitude. Inspect the carrier, the sidebands, and the overmodulation that appears when m > 1.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.description: fm is the baseband frequency, fc is the carrier and m is the modulation index.
controls.indexHint: When m > 1 the envelope crosses zero: overmodulation.

readouts.overmodulatedHint: The envelope inverts and envelope detection distorts

plot.timeDescription: The dashed curves are ±[1 + m cos(2πfm t)], which set the envelope of the modulated signal.
plot.spectrumDescription: Modulation moves the baseband spectrum to either side of fc; each line height depends on m.

insight.title: What to notice
insight.shift: Multiplication moves the baseband spectrum to ±fc; it is a shift, not a copy.
insight.sidebands: Single-tone modulation produces only two sidebands, at fc − fm and fc + fm.
insight.bandwidth: AM bandwidth is twice the baseband bandwidth: B = 2fm.
insight.overmodulation: When m > 1 the envelope goes negative, so simple envelope detection cannot recover the baseband.

experiment.title: Try this
experiment.zero: Set m = 0 and watch the sidebands disappear, leaving only the carrier.
experiment.increase: Move m from 0.5 to 1.4 and compare the envelope with the spectral lines.
experiment.observe: Fix m and change fc: the sideband spacing depends only on fm.

experimentHub.title: Four chapter challenges
experimentHub.subtitle: Every attempt randomises the parameters. Predict, then reveal the plot, then explain it in your own words. A correct answer produces a completion code.

experiment-signal.title: Lab 1: signal classification
experiment-signal.description: A random energy, power or growing signal: decide which class it belongs to.

experiment-time.title: Lab 2: time constant
experiment-time.description: Random τ and k: predict how far the response has travelled at kτ.

experiment-frequency.title: Lab 3: pulse spectrum
experiment-frequency.description: Random pulse width: predict the first zero or the DC value.

experiment-s.title: Lab 4: pole placement
experiment-s.description: Random pole locations: identify the impulse-response shape and stability.

how.title: How completion works
how.description: The plot is a verification tool, not the answer.

seed.title: Random prompt
seed.description: Each new question gives a fresh parameter set and prompt ID.

predict.title: Predict before the plot
predict.description: The plot is hidden until you submit, so you cannot work backwards from the curve.

explain.title: Write the reason
explain.description: At least 20 characters, with a clear because-therefore structure.

code.title: Completion code
code.description: Generated after a correct answer; hand it in together with the prompt ID.

signalBasics.title: Lab 1: classifying signals
signalBasics.subtitle: A signal is generated at random. Decide whether it is an energy signal, a power signal, or neither. Read the expression first.
signalBasics.scenarioDescription: Decide from the expression, without looking at the waveform first.
signalBasics.question: Which class does this signal belong to?
signalBasics.questionFallback: Which class does this signal belong to?

options.both: Both an energy and a power signal

plot.timeDescription: Shown after you submit. Check whether the signal decays to zero at infinity.

insight.title: How to decide
insight.energy: Energy signal: E is finite and positive, and the average power is zero.
insight.power: Power signal: the average power is finite and positive, and the energy is infinite.
insight.neither: The ramp t·u(t) has both infinite energy and infinite power, so it is neither.

timeDomain.title: Lab 2: time constant
timeDomain.subtitle: Given K and τ of a first-order system, predict what percentage of the final value the response has reached at t = kτ. Calculate first, then look.
timeDomain.scenarioDescription: The parameters change every time; estimate from the formula instead of reading the plot.
timeDomain.scenario: K = {gain}, τ = {tau} s. Find the response at t = {k}τ.
timeDomain.question: At t = {k}τ, roughly what percentage of the final value has y(t) reached?
timeDomain.questionFallback: At t = kτ, roughly what percentage of the final value has y(t) reached?

plot.title: Step-response check
plot.description: Shown after you submit; the dashed line is the final value K and the marker sits at kτ.

readouts.valueAtHint: Compute it from the formula, not from the plot

insight.title: Remember these three numbers
insight.multiples: These percentages do not depend on K or τ, only on the multiple k.
insight.gain: K changes only the final value, not the time needed to reach 63.2%.

frequencyDomain.title: Lab 3: spectrum of a rectangular pulse
frequencyDomain.subtitle: Random pulse width τ and height A: predict the first spectral zero or the DC value. The answer comes from the formula, not the plot.
frequencyDomain.scenarioDescription: Write X(f) first, then decide whether the question asks for a zero or the DC value.
frequencyDomain.scenario: x(t) = {a}·rect(t/{tau}), where rect equals 1 for |t| < τ/2.

question.zero: At what frequency is the first positive zero of |X(f)|?
question.dc: What is the spectral value |X(0)| at f = 0?

plot.spectrumDescription: Shown after you submit; the dashed line marks the first zero.

insight.title: The formula gives the answer
insight.sinc: The spectrum of a rectangle is a sinc: X(f) = Aτ·sinc(fτ).
insight.dc: The DC value equals the pulse area Aτ.

sDomain.title: Lab 4: poles decide the response
sDomain.subtitle: Random pole locations: identify the impulse-response shape and stability. Read the s-plane condition before the time curve.
sDomain.scenarioDescription: Decide from the pole locations only; do not look at h(t) first.

scenario.complex: H(s) has a conjugate pole pair at {sigma} ± j{omega}.
scenario.real: H(s) has a double real pole at s = {sigma}.

sDomain.question: Which shape is the impulse response most likely to have?

plot.pzDescription: The shaded region is the ROC; for a causal system it lies right of the rightmost pole.
plot.impulseDescription: Shown after you submit; watch the envelope and the oscillation.

insight.title: How to decide
insight.left: Conjugate poles in the left half-plane → decaying oscillation.
insight.axis: Conjugate poles on the imaginary axis → constant-amplitude oscillation, marginally stable.
insight.right: Conjugate poles in the right half-plane → growing oscillation, unstable.
insight.repeat: A double real pole → a t·e^{σt} shape, still monotonic (it may rise before falling).

quiz.title: Quick quiz
quiz.subtitle: Answer 12 random concept questions in 90 seconds. Correct answers score points and consecutive correct answers earn a streak bonus.

intro.title: Rules
intro.description: Questions span all four chapters; the explanation appears right after each answer.
intro.ruleOne: A correct answer is worth 10 points; each consecutive correct answer adds +2 (up to +10).
intro.ruleTwo: Wrong answers lose no points, but the streak resets.
intro.ruleThree: Time-up ends the round automatically; unanswered questions do not count toward accuracy. The timer pauses while saving.

question.description: Choose one answer; it cannot be changed after you submit.

result.title: Round complete
result.description: Check the score, then review the misses; the misses are worth more of your time than the score.

review.title: Misses and review
review.description: Every question you answered this round, with the correct answer.
review.empty: No answers were recorded before time ran out.

energy-signal.prompt: Which class does x(t) = e^{−2t}u(t) belong to?
energy-signal.option4: Both an energy and a power signal
energy-signal.explain: The decaying exponential has finite energy and zero average power, so it is an energy signal.

convolution-shift.prompt: If h(t) = δ(t − 2), then y(t) = x(t) * h(t) equals?
convolution-shift.explain: Convolution with a delayed impulse shifts the input right by 2: y(t) = x(t − 2).

step-response.prompt: For a first-order system y(t)=K(1−e^{−t/τ}), at t=τ the response reaches what fraction of its final value?
step-response.explain: 1 − e^{−1} ≈ 0.632, so one time constant reaches 63.2%.

aliasing.prompt: With f0=5 Hz and fs=8 Hz, what apparent frequency appears after aliasing?
aliasing.explain: |5 − 8| = 3 Hz; after sampling the high frequency folds to 3 Hz.

nyquist.prompt: A signal has a highest frequency of 4 kHz. What is the theoretical minimum sampling rate?
nyquist.explain: The Nyquist rate is twice the highest frequency, namely 8 kHz.

square-wave.prompt: What directly makes the even harmonics vanish in a symmetric periodic square wave?
square-wave.explain: Odd symmetry removes the cosine terms; half-wave symmetry then removes the even harmonics.

pulse-spectrum.prompt: As a rectangular pulse gets wider, its main spectral lobe becomes?
pulse-spectrum.explain: Widening in time compresses the spectrum: the main-lobe width scales with 1/τ.

time-constant.prompt: For a first-order system, as τ increases the cutoff frequency fc will?
time-constant.explain: fc = 1/(2πτ), so a larger τ means a narrower bandwidth.

damping.prompt: As the damping ratio ζ of a second-order system increases from 0.3 to 0.7, the overshoot usually?
damping.explain: Overshoot decreases as ζ grows; at ζ ≥ 1 there is no overshoot.

right-half-plane.prompt: A causal rational continuous-time LTI system has a right-half-plane pole (no pole-zero cancellation). Its BIBO stability is?
right-half-plane.explain: A right-half-plane pole contributes a growing exponential, so the system is unstable.

am-bandwidth.prompt: An AM signal whose baseband highest frequency is fm has a bandwidth of about?
am-bandwidth.explain: The upper and lower sidebands each occupy fm, so the total bandwidth is 2fm.

imaginary-axis.prompt: A conjugate pole pair on the imaginary axis corresponds to an impulse response that is?
imaginary-axis.explain: The real part is zero, so the envelope neither decays nor grows: the oscillation has constant amplitude.

courseFlow.title: Before · during · after
courseFlow.subtitle: Connect a 15-minute preview, a 45-minute class, and a 30-minute review. Your checks are saved in this browser.

progress.title: Overall progress
progress.description: Check each item as you finish it; progress is stored only in this browser.
progress.hint: Aim to finish the first 3 items before class, the middle 3 during class, and the last 3 afterwards.

before.title: 15 minutes before class
before.description: Bring one question to class instead of an empty head.

items.read: Skim this chapter's formulas and definitions
items.warmup: Play one quick-quiz round and note what felt fuzzy
items.predict: Make one overlap-area prediction on the convolution page

during.title: 45 minutes in class
during.description: Decide alone, explain in a pair, then look at the demo.

items.challenge: Draw a chapter lab at random and write your prediction first
items.explain: Explain to a partner why the plot looks the way it does

after.title: 30 minutes after class
after.description: Turn 'I saw it' into 'I can say it'.

items.experiment: Finish the chapter lab and record the prompt ID and completion code
items.selfcheck: Reach 80% accuracy in the quick quiz
items.question: Write one question about the next chapter you still want to ask

exit.title: One-minute exit ticket
exit.description: Close with two sentences: one conclusion and one confusion. Copy it to your teacher or the class discussion.
exit.keepPlaceholder: For example: the real part of a pole sets the envelope, the imaginary part sets the oscillation rate.
exit.stuckLabel: One point I still do not understand
exit.stuckPlaceholder: For example: why is a system unstable when the ROC excludes the imaginary axis?

teacher.title: Teacher verification tips
teacher.description: Look at the reasoning, not the code.
teacher.before: Draw 2 students before class and ask them to explain the parameters behind a prompt ID in their own words.
teacher.during: Have students hide the plot, write a prediction, and only then unlock it.
teacher.after: Collect completion codes and reasons; a code is derived from the prompt ID and the correct answer, so it is quick to check.
teacher.code: The same prompt ID must produce the same code; the reasoning must be the student's own wording.
